subject: Chemistry
title: Melanin: The Color of Skin and Hair
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Melanin: The Color of Skin and Hair.

hook.text: One molecule controls human skin color, hair color, and eye color: melanin. More melanin means darker color.

buildup.text: Eumelanin produces brown and black. Pheomelanin produces red and yellow. Your mix determines your coloring.

discovery.text: Melanin absorbs UV radiation, protecting DNA from sun damage. Darker skin evolved near the equator for UV defense.

twist.text: Gray hair isn't gray—it's transparent. Hair loses melanin with age, and light scattering makes it look silver.

climax.text: Albinism results from mutations that prevent melanin production. Without it, skin and eyes have no UV protection.

punchline.text: One pigment family, every shade of human. Melanin is evolution's sunscreen.

quiz.question: Why did darker skin evolve in equatorial regions?
options: More melanin absorbs UV radiation, protecting DNA from sun damage
Darker skin retains more heat in cold nights
Melanin repels tropical insects more effectively

details.summary: Melanin is a complex polymer produced by melanocyte cells that absorbs ultraviolet radiation to protect DNA from sun damage. The ratio of two melanin types, dark eumelanin and red-yellow pheomelanin, determines human skin, hair, and eye color across all populations.
details.whyItMatters: Melanin is humanity's primary photoprotective defense against UV radiation and skin cancer. Understanding its chemistry is central to dermatology, cosmetics, and evolutionary biology.
takeaways: Eumelanin produces dark brown to black coloration in skin and hair
Pheomelanin creates red-yellow tones found in red hair and freckles
Melanin absorbs UV radiation to prevent DNA damage in skin cells

faq.question: Why does human hair turn gray with age?
faq.answer: Melanocyte stem cells in hair follicles gradually deplete with age. As fewer melanocytes remain to inject melanin into growing hair shafts, individual hairs grow without pigment and appear white. The mix of pigmented and unpigmented hairs creates the appearance of gray.

faq.question: Why did different human populations evolve different skin melanin levels?
faq.answer: Populations in high-UV equatorial regions evolved high melanin for UV protection. Those who migrated to low-UV northern latitudes evolved less melanin to allow sufficient UV penetration for vitamin D synthesis. This balance between UV protection and vitamin D needs drove adaptation.
